questions.stem: Expanding along the first row, the determinant $\begin{vmatrix}2&1&3\\0&4&-1\\5&2&1\end{vmatrix}$ has the value
questions.explanation: Expanding along the first row: $2(4\cdot1-(-1)\cdot2)-1(0\cdot1-(-1)\cdot5)+3(0\cdot2-4\cdot5)=2(6)-1(5)+3(-20)=12-5-60=-53$. Each cofactor must carry the alternating signs $+,-,+$.

optionRationale.1: This comes from slipping a sign on the middle term, which turns $-5$ into $+5$ and gives $12+5-60=-43$.
optionRationale.3: This has the right size but the wrong overall sign, as if every product had been given the opposite sign.
optionRationale.4: This comes from taking the last cofactor product as $+60$ instead of $-60$, so $12-5+60=67$.

questions.objective: Evaluate a third-order determinant by expansion

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same order.
A. $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$ for conformable matrices.
B. $AB=BA$ for every pair of square matrices of the same order.
C. $|AB|=|A|\,|B|$ for square matrices of the same order.
D. $(A+B)^T=A^T+B^T$.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The transpose of a product reverses the order, so A is true. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, for example $\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ give different products, so B is false. The determinant of a product is the product of determinants (C) and the transpose of a sum is the sum of transposes (D).

optionRationale.2: B is false because matrix multiplication is generally non-commutative, so any option containing B is wrong.
optionRationale.3: This option contains B, which is false, and it leaves out D, which is a correct property.
optionRationale.4: This option omits C, which is a true property of determinants, so the list is incomplete.

questions.objective: Recall basic properties of transpose, product and determinant

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$ it is found that $A^2=pA+qI$ for scalars $p,q$. The value of $p+q$ is
questions.explanation: For a $2\times2$ matrix, $A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+|A|I=0$. Here the trace is $1+3=4$ and $|A|=3+2=5$, so $A^2=4A-5I$, giving $p=4$ and $q=-5$. Direct multiplication confirms $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-4\\8&7\end{bmatrix}=4A-5I$, so $p+q=-1$.

optionRationale.1: This adds $4$ and $5$, ignoring that the constant term enters as $-|A|\,I$ with a negative sign.
optionRationale.2: This takes $p=-4$ and $q=5$, the negatives of the correct values; the $(1,2)$ entry would then be $+4$ instead of $-4$.
optionRationale.4: This takes $p=-4$ and $q=-5$; the $(1,2)$ entry of $pA+qI$ would then be $+4$, but $A^2$ has $-4$ there.

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-3\\2&5\end{bmatrix}$ the element in the second row and first column of $\operatorname{adj}A$ is
questions.explanation: For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$ the adjoint is $\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$. With $a=4,b=-3,c=2,d=5$ we get $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}5&3\\-2&4\end{bmatrix}$, so the second-row, first-column entry is $-c=-2$.

optionRationale.2: This forgets to change the sign of $c$ when forming the adjoint.
optionRationale.3: This is the entry $-b$ that sits in the first row, second column, not the one asked for.
optionRationale.4: This is the original entry $b$, copied without moving it or changing its sign.

questions.objective: Write the adjoint of a second-order matrix

questions.stem: Using Cramer's rule on $3x-2y=4$ and $2x+y=5$, the value of $2x+3y$ is
questions.explanation: The coefficient determinant is $D=3\cdot1-(-2)\cdot2=7$. Then $D_x=4\cdot1-(-2)\cdot5=14$ and $D_y=3\cdot5-4\cdot2=7$, so $x=14/7=2$ and $y=7/7=1$. Therefore $2x+3y=4+3=7$.

optionRationale.2: This swaps the roles of $x$ and $y$, computing $2(1)+3(2)$.
optionRationale.3: This takes both unknowns equal to 2, which does not satisfy $2x+y=5$.
optionRationale.4: $5$ is just the right-hand side of the second equation, not the value of the required expression.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): If $A$ and $B$ are symmetric matrices of the same order, then $AB$ is always symmetric.
Reason (R): For any two matrices, $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The reason is the standard transpose rule and is true. For symmetric $A,B$ it gives $(AB)^T=BA$, which equals $AB$ only when $A$ and $B$ commute. For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $AB\ne BA$, so the assertion is false.

optionRationale.1: The assertion is not true, so the reason cannot be a correct explanation of it.
optionRationale.2: The assertion is false, so the pair cannot both be true.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true, so this option, which calls it false, is wrong.

questions.objective: Test the symmetry of a product of symmetric matrices

questions.stem: The homogeneous system $kx+y+z=0,\ x+ky+z=0,\ x+y+kz=0$ has a non-trivial solution for certain values of $k$. The sum of all such distinct values of $k$ is
questions.explanation: A non-trivial solution exists only if the coefficient determinant vanishes. That determinant equals $(k-1)^2(k+2)$, since adding all rows gives the common factor $k+2$ and the rest reduces to $(k-1)^2$. So $k=1$ or $k=-2$, and the sum of the distinct values is $1+(-2)=-1$.

optionRationale.1: This counts only the root $k=1$ and misses the root $k=-2$.
optionRationale.2: This takes the second factor as $k-2$, giving roots $1$ and $2$ and so a sum of $3$.
optionRationale.3: This takes the repeated factor as $k+1$ and the other as $k+2$, giving roots $-1$ and $-2$ and so a sum of $-3$.

questions.objective: Find parameter values giving a non-trivial solution of a homogeneous system

questions.stem: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&3\\2&0&1\end{bmatrix}$, the element in the first row and third column of $A^{-1}$ is
questions.explanation: First $|A|=1(1-0)-2(0-6)+0=13$. The $(1,3)$ element of $A^{-1}$ is $C_{31}/|A|$ where $C_{31}=+\begin{vmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{vmatrix}=6$. Hence the element is $6/13$; remember the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, so row and column indices swap.

optionRationale.2: The cofactor $C_{31}$ has sign $(-1)^{3+1}=+1$, so the negative sign here is a mistake.
optionRationale.3: This uses $C_{13}=-2$, the cofactor in the same position, instead of $C_{31}$, forgetting the transpose in the adjoint.
optionRationale.4: This uses the size of $C_{13}$ with its sign lost and again forgets the transpose.
